# Education in Norway
Education in Norway is compulsory for children aged 6 to 16, encompassing elementary (barneskole, ages 6–12) and lower secondary (ungdomsskole, ages 13–16) school, which together are referred to as grunnskole (‘foundation school’). The Norwegian school system then continues with upper secondary education (videregående skole, ages 16–19), which is not compulsory but widely attended, primarily through public schools. The education system features a progression from basic literacy and social skills in the early years, to formal grading and subject specialization in later years. Vocational and general studies form the main tracks at upper secondary level, and a reform (Kunnskapsløftet) in 2006 strengthened IT integration and cross-path flexibility. Private schools are rare and heavily regulated, requiring government approval and government grants, and cannot select students by ability.
Higher education in Norway generally requires the completion of upper secondary studies, with universities, university colleges, and a limited number of private institutions offering bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral degrees. Admissions to higher education are competitive, often based on secondary school grades, with state-run universities predominating. Education providers are independently responsible for instruction, research, and quality assurance (overseen by NOKUT). Special education for students with disabilities is integrated into public schools, with support services available. The academic year runs from mid-August to June, includes two semesters, and schools observe multiple holidays and breaks throughout the year.
